Then schedule no‑phone reps across times of day and mild stressors to defeat context tethering, so when the chime is gone, the calm remains (per Bouton 2002). If you keep an app, use it as training wheels on a timer—scaffold practice when calm, not as an emergency exit—and progressively remove prompts as your body learns to carry the skill.

candidate.hook: Your hips aren’t the limiter—your ankles are. Tight dorsiflexion is what makes your heels pop, your chest dump, and your squat stall above parallel.
candidate.frame: We’ve all chased depth and felt our heels want to peel and our torso tip—so we’re reading the squat from the ankle up. Through that lens, dorsiflexion—not hip mobility—sets how deep we can actually sit.
candidate.payload: In a deep squat, your knees must translate forward to keep your center of mass over midfoot; that forward tibial progression is ankle dorsiflexion, and when the talocrural joint won’t allow it, you compensate by lifting the heels, turning the feet out, pronating, and dumping the torso to stay balanced (per Schoenfeld 2010). When dorsiflexion is experimentally restricted, lifters reliably achieve less depth and exhibit greater trunk lean, shifting demand up the chain to the hips and lumbar spine—classic ankle-driven compensations (per Macrum et al. 2012). By contrast, adding a raised heel or weightlifting shoe—which reduces required dorsiflexion—consistently increases depth and reduces forward torso angle without any change in hip mobility (per Sinclair et al. 2014). Mechanically, the knee angle you can achieve over the foot sets how low the pelvis can drop between the femurs; if the ankle limits knee travel, the hips can be mobile yet still can’t get you below parallel without balance trade-offs (per Schoenfeld 2010). A quick predictor is the weight-bearing lunge test: it’s reliable for indexing dorsiflexion and relates to how far your knees can travel in a squat, which closely mirrors your achievable depth (per Bennell et al. 1998). Practical takeaway: improve dorsiflexion with soleus-biased calf work and posterior talar glide mobilizations, and use heel-elevated variations or weightlifting shoes while it catches up—hip work helps, but the ankle is the rate-limiter for most depth issues.

A heel lift is just a doorstop propping that doorway open, letting you sink lower without changing your hip mobility.

candidate.topic: Why ankle flexibility predicts squat depth more than hip mobility
candidate.hook: Your hips aren’t stopping your squat—your ankles are. If your heels want to lift and your chest tips forward, it’s ankle flexibility capping your depth.
candidate.frame: We’re reading squat depth through the ankles, not the hips—the heel peel and forward torso are the tells. If you’ve been chasing hip openers without deeper depth, we’re treating dorsiflexion and tibia angle as the real gatekeepers.
candidate.payload:
Ankle dorsiflexion is the bottleneck for depth because the tibia must travel forward over the foot to keep your center of mass over midfoot; when the talocrural joint or soleus/Achilles are stiff, your options are heel peel or more torso lean. Restricting dorsiflexion during squats reliably reduces knee bend and increases trunk lean and hip flexion—classic “hips back, chest down” (per Macrum et al. 2012). Squat biomechanics show tibia angle and torso angle are coupled: if the knees can move forward (via available dorsiflexion), you can stay more upright and sit deeper; if they can’t, the hips have to travel back to keep balance, capping depth regardless of hip “opener” work (per Escamilla 2001). If you pass hip ER/IR screens but fail a simple knee-to-wall test, that’s the tell that dorsiflexion—not “tight hips”—is your gatekeeper.

To change it, train dorsiflexion directly: long‑lever calf eccentrics and end‑range isometrics for the soleus, ankle joint mobilizations driving the talus posteriorly, and knee‑forward squat patterns (e.g., goblet squats with a heel wedge). You should see immediate depth gains with a small heel lift because it reduces the dorsiflexion requirement mechanically; then make it stick by loading knee‑forward squats and split squats in the new range. Re-test your bodyweight squat after ankle work—if depth and torso angle improve without any hip stretching, you’ve found the true constraint.

candidate.topic: Why ankle flexibility predicts squat depth more than hip mobility
candidate.hook: You’re blaming tight hips for a shallow squat, but the real depth governor sits below your calves. When your ankles won’t let your knees glide forward, your hips have nowhere to go.
candidate.frame: We’re looking at squat depth through tibia travel and dorsiflexion—the knee’s forward glide that frees the hips to drop. With that lens, the fixes shift from hip openers to ankle prep and simple setup tweaks.
candidate.payload: Squat depth is governed by how far your tibia can glide forward over the foot; limited ankle dorsiflexion forces your center of mass backward, so you compensate with early hip hinge and trunk lean, capping depth or dumping flexion into the lumbar spine (per Escamilla 2001). In functional screens, weight-bearing dorsiflexion measured by the lunge test reliably tracks with deep-squat quality, and reduced dorsiflexion is linked to altered squat mechanics and valgus strategies (per Powden, Hoch & Hoch 2015; Mauntel et al. 2014). Practical fixes: raise the heels with lifters or a small wedge to instantly lower the dorsiflexion demand and allow more knee travel; slightly widen stance and toe out to match hip structure while keeping pressure over midfoot; and prep ankles with soleus-focused calf mobilizations and end-range dorsiflexion drills like knee-to-wall pulses. Test, don’t guess—recheck a weight-bearing lunge test before and after ankle work to confirm that more tibial travel actually buys you more squat depth (per Powden, Hoch & Hoch 2015).
candidate.bridge: Squatting with limited ankle dorsiflexion is like trying to sit deep while wearing ski boots: when your shins can’t glide forward, you’re forced to kick the hips back and lean the torso, and your spine pays the price before your depth does. Free up the “boots” and the knees can travel, letting you drop straight down instead of tipping.
